title: Paika: service, community and Odia heritage
lead: Who were the Paikas—and does the name describe a military role, a caste or a living tradition? The answer begins with land and service, then follows the different histories that gathered around the name.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy

paragraphs.text: In the Khurda kingdom, Paikas cultivated service lands and answered their chiefs when military or policing duties required them. Land supported their service. The district history names recruits from several communities, including Chasa, Pana, Kandara and Bauri, as well as Muslims. Paika therefore cannot be treated as a historical synonym for one caste.
paragraphs.locator: paragraphs on service lands and recruitment, web lines21–22

paragraphs.text: The same account distinguishes guards carrying sword and shield, matchlock users sent on expeditions, and bow-and-arrow fighters. Duty and equipment distinguished these groups. They establish neither caste genealogy nor a founding date.
paragraphs.locator: web lines23–27; final sentence analytical scope limit

paragraphs.text: Akio Tanabe’s study gives a concrete example from late-eighteenth-century Garh Manitri in Khurda. A payment record includes Khandayats among foot soldiers, alongside a cowherd sub-chief and three Muslim fort watchmen. Military musicians and other workers also supported the establishment. The connection with Khandayat is real; the record also shows why the two names cannot simply replace each other.
paragraphs.locator: section Pāika and Non-Pāika Participants, web586–588, footnote62

paragraphs.text: Tanabe explains that military and administrative positions could become hereditary, carrying entitlements to land and payment. Access by people of different backgrounds did not mean equality: ranks and remuneration differed sharply. This offers a historical mechanism for inherited service identities, rather than a story of a single ruler creating one caste for one purpose.
paragraphs.locator: web582–589; mechanism synthesis marked as interpretation

paragraphs.text: The surviving records discussed here establish a working institution by the late eighteenth century. They do not identify its first founder. Family accounts of ancestors gaining office through bravery belong in the history too, but Tanabe labels his Garh Manitri account a legend based on interviews; it should not be converted into a dated event.
paragraphs.locator: web574–581; evidence boundary not first-attestation claim

sections.title: The name changes with place and period

paragraphs.text: Southern Odisha needs its own account. The Koraput Gazetteer reproduces an 1891 description of Paiko as an occupational name for armed retainers of Odia chiefs in Ganjam and Vizagapatam, drawn from different castes and holding service land. It also discusses Paiko and Kottia Paiko as regional community names. Those passages preserve different uses of a related term; they are not permission to merge every community carrying it.
paragraphs.locator: printed140, PDF166, Paiko and Kottia Paiko headings

paragraphs.text: The gazetteer also repeats older colonial classifications. Such records help trace how officials described people, but claims about ancestry, social rank or community character need critical checking and present-day community testimony. This article concentrates on the Khurda service system and its wider connections; it does not settle every Paiko community’s history.
paragraphs.locator: printed139–141; editorial boundary grounded in quoted colonial descriptions

sections.title: Why the service system mattered in 1817

paragraphs.text: After the British takeover, the loss of service lands and oppressive revenue collection damaged that relationship between cultivation, military duty and livelihood. Jagabandhu’s own dispossession made his grievance especially visible. Khordha’s history describes Kandhas arriving from Ghumsur in March 1817 and Paikas joining them under Jagabandhu. The sequence matters: tribal participants were actors in the uprising, not merely a supporting crowd added to someone else’s story.

The Government of India’s bicentenary account describes the rebellion spreading to Puri, Pipli, Cuttack and other places, with participation beyond the militia. It identifies Baxi Jagabandhu as the hereditary military chief and records British suppression after the initial rebel successes. Paika heritage includes this resistance, but 1817 was a crisis in an existing institution, not the creation of the Paikas.

Paika heritage also lives in movement and music. Khordha’s cultural account describes village groups performing Paika Nrutya, a battle dance, during Dussehra. It names dholak, nagara, shehnai and dhak as accompaniment. The district account relates the word Paika to padatika, meaning infantry. This is a locally documented connection between martial memory, performance and the festival calendar; it does not establish an unbroken choreography from the eighteenth century.

To understand an akhada in its own place, begin with the people who sustain it. What do they call their practice in Odia? Who taught them, which occasions bring them together, and what has changed between generations? A named teacher, a remembered training place and a carefully described movement can make heritage more tangible than a sweeping claim of antiquity.

For family and community histories, keep the same care: record the place, the period, the name people use for themselves and the evidence behind an origin account. An inherited story deserves to be heard in its own words. Whether it describes a military appointment, a caste identity or a local tradition is a question to investigate, not a distinction to erase.
